bounded_predicate: Report when with exactly two entries, an else, and no entry containing multiple comma-separated conditions, unless ignoreWhenContainingVariableDeclaration is true and the subject is a KtProperty. Entity.from(when), no type binding.
selection_rationale: Adds a binary-branch convention not covered by existing rules. Meaningful grouped alternatives, exhaustive boolean arms and a single-evaluation subject binding constrain the proposal; the real option warrants the fourth case.

positive.intent: A binary branch with one condition and one default is an explicit if-versus-when readability convention. It is not a correctness assertion.

sources.Case.kt:
package corpus.binarywhen

fun label(code: Int): String = if (code == 0) "empty" else "present"

negative.intent: An equivalent binary conditional on a stable integer parameter uses if; the selected rule remains active.

suppression.intent: Genuine file-scoped upstream suppression only on a package-isolated positive copy. The byte-identical unsuppressed Case.kt keeps all authored ranges; no host filtering or ktChecker-ID alias.

controls.intent: Grouped alternatives share an outcome but there is more than one condition in the first entry; this explicit readability boundary is not just an entry-count test.
The exhaustive boolean choice intentionally has no else; the rule requires an else and must not manufacture one.

A when subject declares a value reused in the default branch, preserving a single callback evaluation and local scope. Default false still reports; no semantics-preserving simple if rewrite is assumed.
The actual ignoreWhenContainingVariableDeclaration option exempts the byte-identical subject-declaration source while leaving the rule active. It preserves a legitimate one-read scoped idiom.

limitations: Binary when can be intentional. No architecture/style default is changed; this remains opt-in info/intent-dependent.
The fixture uses Kotlin when-subject declaration syntax; no parser/compiler execution has yet qualified these bytes. Future version variants and Common/Native execution remain unqualified.
The option is a syntactic subject-declaration exemption, not call-effect, branch exhaustiveness or evaluation-count proof.
